title: Healthy Teeth for Life
summary: What different teeth do, how bacteria, sugar, and acid cause cavities, and the daily habits, foods, and dentist visits that keep teeth healthy, including the traditional miswak.
poll: Brushing your teeth is more important than what you eat and drink.

versions.title: Take Care of Your Teeth
versions.text:
Grin! Your teeth help you eat. They help you talk. They help you grin.

Kids have 20 baby teeth. At age six or so, they start to fall out. Then new teeth grow in. Adults have 32 teeth. These teeth must last all your life!

Front teeth bite and cut. Back teeth crush and grind. Each tooth has a hard coat. It is called enamel. It is the hardest part of you.

Germs live in your mouth. They make a thin film. It is called plaque. It is sticky. The germs eat sugar. Then they make acid. Acid can make a hole in a tooth. This is a cavity. It can hurt!

So brush two times a day. Brush for two full minutes. Floss once a day. Floss gets food out from where teeth touch. See the dentist two times a year.

Eat less candy. Drink lots of water. Milk and cheese help, too.

Long ago, people in Arabia used a stick to clean their teeth. It is a miswak. It comes from a tree. Some still use it.

versions.title: Take Care of Your Teeth
versions.text:
Smile! Your teeth do a lot for you. They help you eat. They help you talk. And they help you smile.

Kids have 20 baby teeth. At about age six, the baby teeth start to fall out. New, big teeth grow in. Grown-ups have 32 teeth. These teeth must last for the rest of your life!

Your front teeth bite and cut food. Your back teeth crush and grind it. Each tooth has a hard coat on the outside. It is called enamel. Enamel is the hardest thing in your whole body.

Tiny germs live in your mouth. They form a thin, sticky film on your teeth. This film is called plaque. The germs in plaque eat sugar. Then they make acid. Acid can make a hole in a tooth. The hole is called a cavity. It can hurt.

To keep your teeth strong, brush them two times a day. Brush for two whole minutes. Floss once a day to clean between your teeth. Go to the dentist two times a year.

Eat less candy. Drink water, not soda. Milk and cheese help make teeth strong.

Long ago, people in Arabia cleaned their teeth with a stick called a miswak. It comes from the arak tree. Lots of people still use it.

versions.title: Take Care of Your Teeth
versions.text:
Every time you smile, take a bite of food, or say a word, you are using your teeth. They are small, but they work hard all day long.

Children have 20 baby teeth. At about age six, these teeth begin to fall out, and larger adult teeth grow in to take their place. Adults have 32 teeth. These teeth must last for the rest of your life, so caring for them is important.

Different teeth have different jobs. The sharp front teeth bite and cut food, while the wide back teeth crush and grind it. Each tooth is covered by a hard outer layer called enamel. In fact, enamel is the hardest material in the human body.

Tiny germs live in every mouth. They form a thin, sticky film on the teeth called plaque. When you eat sugar, the germs in plaque eat it too. Then they make acid. Over time, this acid can wear a small hole in a tooth. The hole is called a cavity, and it can be painful.

To protect your teeth, brush them twice a day for two minutes each time. Floss once a day to remove food and plaque from between your teeth. Visit the dentist for a checkup two times a year.

What you eat matters, too. Eat fewer sweets, and drink water instead of soda. Milk and cheese help keep teeth strong.

For hundreds of years, people in Arabia have used a miswak to clean their teeth. It is a thin stick cut from the arak tree, and many people still use one today.

versions.title: Healthy Teeth, Happy Smile
versions.text:
Every time you smile, bite into an apple, or say hello, you use your teeth. They are small, but they do important work all day long.

Children have 20 baby teeth. At about age six, these teeth begin to fall out, and larger adult teeth grow in to replace them. Most adults have 32 teeth. Since these teeth must last for the rest of your life, caring for them is a smart choice.

Different teeth have different jobs. The flat front teeth, called incisors, cut food. The pointed canines next to them tear food. The wide molars at the back crush and grind food so you can swallow it. Each tooth is covered by enamel, a hard outer layer. Enamel is the hardest material in the human body.

Tiny living things called bacteria live in every mouth. They form plaque, a thin, sticky film on the teeth. When you eat or drink something sugary, the bacteria feed on the sugar and make acid. Over time, the acid can wear away enamel and make a hole called a cavity.

To protect your teeth, brush twice a day for two minutes with a toothpaste that has fluoride. Fluoride helps make enamel stronger. Floss once a day to clean between your teeth. Visit a dentist every six months for a checkup.

What you eat and drink matters, too. Sweets and sugary drinks feed bacteria, so enjoy them less often. Water, milk, and cheese are good choices for healthy teeth.

For hundreds of years, people in Arabia have cleaned their teeth with a miswak, a thin stick cut from the arak tree. Scientists have found that it has natural substances that fight germs.

versions.title: Healthy Teeth for Life
versions.text:
Every time you smile, bite into a crisp apple, or greet a friend, you depend on your teeth. Although they are relatively small, they perform important work from the moment you wake up until you fall asleep. Keeping them healthy therefore requires consistent attention every single day, not just once in a while.

Children usually have 20 baby teeth, which begin to loosen and fall out at about age six, as larger permanent teeth gradually emerge to replace them. Most adults ultimately have 32 permanent teeth, and because the human body cannot grow another set, caring for them properly is an essential lifelong responsibility.

Different teeth have specialized functions that work together during every meal. The flat front teeth, called incisors, slice food, while the pointed canines beside them tear it apart. The broad molars at the back crush and grind it so that you can swallow comfortably. Every tooth is protected by enamel, a hard outer layer made mostly of minerals, which is the toughest substance in the human body.

Microscopic organisms called bacteria inhabit every mouth, where they form plaque, a thin, sticky film that gradually accumulates on the teeth. Whenever you eat or drink something sugary, these bacteria feed on the sugar and release acid as a waste product. Over time, this acid can erode the enamel. The resulting decay eventually produces a hole called a cavity, which may become extremely painful and require professional treatment.

To protect your teeth, dentists recommend brushing twice daily for two minutes with a toothpaste containing fluoride, a substance that helps strengthen enamel. Flossing once a day removes plaque from between the teeth, where a toothbrush cannot reach. Visiting a dentist every six months for a thorough examination and professional cleaning allows developing problems to be identified long before they become serious.

Diet is equally important. Sweets and sugary beverages nourish harmful bacteria, so they should be enjoyed only occasionally, whereas water, milk, and cheese are excellent choices for maintaining healthy teeth.

For centuries, people in the Arabian Peninsula have cleaned their teeth with a miswak, a slender stick cut from the arak tree. Scientists have discovered that it contains natural antibacterial substances that combat harmful germs, which demonstrates that traditional practices can sometimes be supported by modern scientific research.

versions.title: Healthy Teeth for Life
versions.text:
Every time you smile, bite into a crisp apple, or greet a friend, you depend on your teeth, which, although relatively small, perform indispensable work from the moment you awaken until you fall asleep. Consequently, keeping them healthy requires consistent and deliberate attention every single day.

Children typically possess 20 primary, or baby, teeth, which begin to loosen and fall out at approximately age six as larger permanent teeth gradually emerge to replace them. Most adults ultimately have 32 permanent teeth, and because the human body cannot generate an additional set, maintaining them properly represents an essential lifelong responsibility.

Different teeth have specialized functions that operate cooperatively during every meal. The flat front teeth, called incisors, slice food, while the pointed canines positioned beside them tear it apart, and the broad molars at the back crush and grind it so that you can swallow comfortably. Every tooth is protected by enamel, a durable outer layer composed predominantly of minerals, which is considered the toughest substance in the human body.

Microscopic organisms called bacteria inhabit every mouth, where they form plaque, a thin, sticky film that gradually accumulates on the teeth. Whenever you consume something sugary, these bacteria metabolize the sugar and release acid as a waste product. Over time, this acid can erode the enamel, and the resulting decay eventually produces a hole called a cavity, which may become extremely painful and require professional treatment.

To protect your teeth, dental experts recommend brushing twice daily for two minutes with a toothpaste containing fluoride, a substance that helps strengthen and repair enamel. Flossing once a day removes plaque from between the teeth, where a toothbrush cannot reach, and visiting a dentist every six months for a thorough examination and professional cleaning allows developing problems to be identified long before they become serious.

Nutrition is equally significant, because sweets and sugary beverages nourish harmful bacteria and should therefore be enjoyed only occasionally, whereas water, milk, and cheese are excellent choices for maintaining healthy teeth.

For centuries, inhabitants of the Arabian Peninsula have cleaned their teeth with a miswak, a slender stick cut from the arak tree. Scientists have discovered that it contains natural antibacterial substances that combat harmful germs, which demonstrates that traditional practices can occasionally be confirmed by contemporary scientific research.

versions.title: Healthy Teeth for Life
versions.text:
Every smile, every bite into a crisp apple, and every spoken greeting relies upon the teeth, modest structures that nonetheless perform indispensable functions from the moment of waking until the moment of sleep; sustaining their health therefore demands deliberate, consistent attention rather than sporadic concern.

Children typically possess twenty primary teeth, which begin to loosen and exfoliate at approximately six years of age as the larger permanent dentition gradually emerges to replace them. Because the human body is incapable of regenerating a subsequent set once the permanent teeth have erupted, their lifelong preservation constitutes an essential responsibility rather than an optional habit.

Each category of tooth fulfills a specialized mechanical function during mastication. The flat anterior incisors slice food into manageable portions, the pointed canines positioned adjacent to them tear more resistant material, and the broad posterior molars crush and grind food sufficiently for comfortable swallowing. Every tooth is encased within enamel, a remarkably durable outer layer composed predominantly of mineral compounds and recognized as the hardest substance within the human body.

Countless microscopic bacteria inhabit the oral cavity, where they aggregate into plaque, an adhesive film that accumulates gradually upon the tooth surface. Whenever sugary substances are consumed, these resident bacteria metabolize the sugar and release acidic byproducts as a consequence. Over time, this acid progressively erodes the mineral structure of the enamel, and the resulting decay eventually manifests as a cavity, a lesion capable of producing considerable pain and necessitating professional intervention.

To mitigate this process, dental professionals consistently recommend brushing twice daily for a minimum of two minutes using fluoride toothpaste, a formulation that reinforces and remineralizes enamel. Daily flossing removes accumulated plaque from interdental spaces inaccessible to a toothbrush, while biannual dental examinations enable the early identification of emerging problems before they progress into serious complications.

Dietary choices exert a comparably significant influence, since confectionery and sugary beverages nourish cariogenic bacteria and should therefore be consumed only occasionally, whereas water, milk, and cheese represent considerably more beneficial alternatives for sustaining dental health.

For many centuries, inhabitants of the Arabian Peninsula have employed the miswak, a slender stick derived from the arak tree, as a traditional instrument of oral hygiene. Contemporary scientific investigation has revealed that this implement contains naturally occurring antibacterial compounds capable of combating harmful microorganisms, a discovery that illustrates how longstanding traditional practices can occasionally receive validation through modern empirical research. Taken together, these daily habits, sensible dietary choices, and regular professional care form the foundation upon which a healthy, lasting smile genuinely depends.

versions.title: Healthy Teeth for Life
versions.text:
Every smile exchanged, every incisive bite taken from a crisp apple, and every articulated greeting depends fundamentally upon the teeth, anatomically modest structures that nonetheless discharge indispensable functions continuously from the moment of waking until the onset of sleep. Consequently, the preservation of dental health necessitates deliberate, systematic vigilance rather than intermittent or casual attention.

Children typically possess twenty deciduous, or primary, teeth, which begin to loosen and exfoliate at approximately six years of age as the considerably larger permanent dentition gradually emerges to supplant them. Because the human organism possesses no physiological capacity to regenerate a subsequent set once the permanent teeth have fully erupted, their sustained preservation constitutes an essential, lifelong obligation rather than a discretionary habit.

Each morphological category of tooth performs a specialized mechanical function during the process of mastication. The flat anterior incisors shear food into manageable fragments, the pointed canines positioned adjacent to them lacerate more resistant material, and the broad posterior molars pulverize and triturate food sufficiently for comfortable deglutition. Every individual tooth is encased within enamel, an extraordinarily durable outer stratum composed predominantly of mineral compounds and universally recognized as the most resilient biological substance within the human organism.

Innumerable microscopic bacteria colonize the oral cavity, where they coalesce into plaque, an adhesive biofilm that accumulates incrementally upon the dental surface. Whenever saccharine substances are ingested, these resident microorganisms metabolize the available sugar and release acidic metabolic byproducts as a consequence of this process. Over an extended interval, this acidic byproduct progressively erodes the mineralized structure of the enamel, and the resultant decay eventually manifests as a cavity, a lesion capable of generating considerable pain and necessitating professional therapeutic intervention.

To mitigate this cariogenic process, dental practitioners consistently advocate brushing twice daily for a minimum duration of two minutes using fluoride-formulated toothpaste, a compound that reinforces and remineralizes compromised enamel. Daily flossing removes accumulated plaque from interdental regions inaccessible to conventional toothbrush bristles, while biannual dental examinations facilitate the early identification of incipient pathology before it progresses into a considerably more serious complication.

Dietary composition exerts a comparably substantial influence upon dental integrity, since confectionery and sugar-laden beverages nourish cariogenic bacterial populations and should therefore be consumed only sporadically, whereas water, milk, and cheese constitute considerably more advantageous alternatives for sustaining long-term oral health.

For numerous centuries, inhabitants of the Arabian Peninsula have employed the miswak, a slender stick derived from the arak tree, as a traditional implement of oral hygiene, wielding it long before any scientific understanding of bacterial pathology existed. Contemporary empirical investigation has subsequently revealed that this traditional implement contains naturally occurring antibacterial compounds capable of combating pathogenic microorganisms, a discovery that illustrates how longstanding traditional practices can, upon rigorous scientific scrutiny, occasionally receive genuine empirical validation.

MID.prompt: Explain how a cavity forms and two ways to prevent one. Use details from the article.
checklist: I explained the steps that cause a cavity.
I gave two ways to prevent cavities.
I used at least two key words, such as bacteria or fluoride.
MID.modelAnswer: A cavity forms when bacteria in your mouth feed on sugar from food and drinks and produce acid, and over time this acid weakens the enamel and creates a hole, even in a strong molar. One way to prevent a cavity is to brush twice a day with toothpaste that has fluoride, since fluoride makes enamel stronger. Another way is to visit a dentist every six months so any early damage can be caught and treated.

HIGH.prompt: Which daily habit do you think does the most to prevent tooth decay? Explain your choice using evidence from the article.
checklist: I supported my choice with evidence from the article.
I used at least two key words correctly.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I think brushing with fluoride toothpaste does the most to prevent tooth decay. Fluoride is a mineral that strengthens enamel, which matters most for permanent adult teeth that must last a lifetime, so a stronger enamel layer resists the acid that would otherwise erode it. Flossing, visiting the dentist, and even the traditional miswak stick's antibacterial substances all help too, but none of them rebuild enamel the way fluoride does, which is why I chose brushing as the most important daily habit.
